_about: Plain-English help shown in the settings panel's 'What is this?' dropdowns. Edit freely: keys are stage, stage.option or stage.option.knob (stt.mode etc. for the shared speech-to-text settings). Fields: what (always), higher / lower (what turning it up or down feels like), start (a sensible value).

trigger.what: Decides WHEN the system starts listening for a command. Without a trigger it would have to transcribe everything said in the room. The trigger is the 'it's talking to me' moment: either you hold a button, or you say the robot's name (the wake word).

vad.what: VAD stands for Voice Activity Detection. Every 32 milliseconds it looks at the sound and answers one question: is someone speaking right now, or is this just silence or background noise? The rest of the system relies on it to know when your command starts, and when you've stopped talking.

endpoint.what: Decides when you have FINISHED your command (also called 'end-of-turn detection' or 'endpointing'). It is the hardest part: decide too early and it cuts you off mid-sentence ('move left... [cut]'); wait too long and every command feels slow. Most of the delay you feel comes from this setting.

stt.what: Speech-to-text: the engine that turns your recorded words into written text. The engines differ in speed, accuracy, and whether they can show words live while you are still speaking.

device.what: Which processor the speech engines run on. 'auto' picks the best one the computer has: the Apple GPU (metal) on this Mac, an NVIDIA graphics card (cuda) on the lab PC, otherwise the ordinary processor (cpu). Leave on auto unless you are testing speed on a particular processor.

presets.what: A preset is a saved copy of every setting on this page, with a name. Load one to switch the whole set-up in one click (for example 'baseline' or 'smart-turn'); save your own when you find a combination you like. Presets used for reported results should not be changed afterwards: save a new one instead.

trigger.push_to_talk.what: Hold the 'Hold to talk' button (or the space bar, with this page focused) while you speak. The most reliable trigger: it never wakes by mistake and never misses. Good for noisy rooms and for testing.

trigger.openwakeword.what: Hands-free: a small model listens all the time for the wake word (for example 'Truffles') and starts listening when it hears it. The button does nothing in this mode.

trigger.both.what: Either works: say the wake word, OR hold the button. The sensible everyday choice: hands-free normally, and the button as a backup when it's noisy or the wake word isn't catching you. The wake-word settings below apply.

vad.silero.what: Silero VAD: a small neural network trained on lots of speech and noise. Good at ignoring background noise (fans, typing). The recommended choice.

vad.webrtc.what: WebRTC VAD: the classic rule-based detector from Google's video-calling software. Very fast but easily fooled by steady noise such as fans. Kept as a simple baseline to compare against.

endpoint.silence.what: The simplest rule: you've finished when you've been silent for a set time. Predictable, but it can't tell a thinking pause ('move left... ten centimetres') from the end of a command.

endpoint.adaptive.what: Our own smarter version of the silence rule. It reads the words heard so far: if you stopped on a word that suggests more is coming ('move up by...', 'x ten y...', a number with no unit yet), it waits longer; otherwise it waits only a short time. Needs speech-to-text in 'streaming' mode to see the words as you speak; otherwise it behaves like the silence rule.

endpoint.smart_turn.what: Smart Turn: a trained model that listens to HOW you speak (tone, rhythm, falling pitch at the end of a sentence), not just to silence, to judge whether you've finished. After a short pause it asks the model; if the model says 'not finished', it keeps listening.

endpoint.ptt_release.what: You've finished when you let go of the button. No guessing at all, so it's the fastest and never cuts you off: the reference the other methods are compared with. Only makes sense with a button (push-to-talk or both).

stt.parakeet.what: NVIDIA Parakeet: very fast and very accurate, with punctuation and capital letters. Runs on this Mac's GPU. The recommended engine.

stt.whisper_cpp.what: OpenAI's Whisper model, in a fast C++ version that runs on the Mac GPU. Well known and accurate; slightly behind Parakeet on these tests.

stt.faster_whisper.what: The same Whisper model in a different implementation, which is fast on NVIDIA graphics cards (the lab PC) but slow on this Mac, where it can only use the ordinary processor (about 1 second per command).

stt.moonshine.what: Moonshine: a small engine designed to transcribe while you're still speaking. Use it in 'streaming' mode; in 'batch' mode it tends to invent words around short commands.

trigger.openwakeword.model.what: Which wake word to listen for. 'models/truffles.onnx' is our own trained 'Truffles' model; the others are ready-made phrases from openWakeWord ('hey_jarvis' means 'hey Jarvis').

trigger.openwakeword.threshold.what: How sure the model must be (a score from 0 to 1) before it counts as hearing the wake word. Every 80 ms it gives a score; at or above this number counts as a hit.
trigger.openwakeword.threshold.higher: Fewer false wake-ups (it ignores 'trouble'), but it may miss you, especially if you're quiet or far away.
trigger.openwakeword.threshold.lower: Catches you more easily, but wakes by mistake more often.
trigger.openwakeword.threshold.start: 0.5. Try 0.3 if it misses you, 0.7 if it wakes by mistake.

trigger.openwakeword.patience.what: How many hits IN A ROW (each 80 ms apart) are needed before it wakes. With 1, a single confident moment is enough. With 2 or 3, the wake word has to score highly for a little longer, which filters out brief sounds that happen to look like it.
trigger.openwakeword.patience.higher: Fewer false wake-ups from short sounds, but slightly slower to react, and short or fast 'Truffles' may be missed.
trigger.openwakeword.patience.lower: Reacts as soon as it hears the word.
trigger.openwakeword.patience.start: 1. Try 2 if it wakes on random short noises.

trigger.openwakeword.cooldown_s.what: After it wakes, how long (seconds) it ignores the wake word. Stops one 'Truffles' from triggering twice, and stops your command from re-waking it straight away.
trigger.openwakeword.cooldown_s.higher: No double triggers, but you must wait longer before you can wake it again.
trigger.openwakeword.cooldown_s.lower: You can wake it again sooner, with a small risk of one 'Truffles' counting twice.

vad.silero.threshold.what: How sure Silero must be (0 to 1) that a 32 ms slice is speech before it counts as speech.
vad.silero.threshold.higher: Ignores more background noise, but quiet speech or soft word endings may be treated as silence, which can make the system think you've stopped.
vad.silero.threshold.lower: Picks up quiet speech, but may treat noise (a fan, a cough) as speech, so it waits longer before deciding you've finished.

vad.silero.min_speech_ms.what: How long a sound must keep sounding like speech (milliseconds) before it counts as the START of your command. Stops a click, a cough or a door bang from starting a command.
vad.silero.min_speech_ms.higher: More robust to short noises, but very short commands ('stop') take a moment longer to register.
vad.silero.min_speech_ms.lower: Reacts to the very first sound.

vad.webrtc.aggressiveness.what: How strict WebRTC is about calling something speech, from 0 (lenient) to 3 (strict).
vad.webrtc.aggressiveness.higher: Treats more noise as non-speech; may miss quiet speech.
vad.webrtc.aggressiveness.lower: Treats almost any sound as speech, including background noise.

vad.webrtc.frame_ms.what: The size of the slices WebRTC looks at: 10, 20 or 30 milliseconds. Larger slices give it more sound to judge each time.

vad.webrtc.threshold.what: WebRTC judges several small slices inside each 32 ms piece of audio. This is the fraction of them that must be speech for the piece to count as speech.

vad.webrtc.min_speech_ms.what: Same as for Silero: how long speech must last before it counts as the start of your command.

endpoint.silence.silence_ms.what: How long you must be silent (milliseconds) before it decides you've finished. This number is added straight onto the delay you feel after every command.
endpoint.silence.silence_ms.higher: Lets you pause to think mid-command without being cut off, but every command feels slower.
endpoint.silence.silence_ms.lower: Snappier, but a natural pause ('move left... ten centimetres') ends the command too early.
endpoint.silence.silence_ms.start: 700 ms. 400 feels quick but cuts pauses; 1000 is safe but slow.

endpoint.adaptive.short_silence_ms.what: The wait used when your words so far look like a complete command ('move up five centimetres.').

endpoint.adaptive.long_silence_ms.what: The wait used when your words so far look unfinished (they end in a word from the 'continue words' list, or a number with no unit yet).
endpoint.adaptive.long_silence_ms.higher: More time to think in the middle of a command.

endpoint.adaptive.continue_words.what: Words that suggest more is coming if you stop on them ('move up BY...', 'go TO...'). Comma-separated. Add words you often pause after.
endpoint.adaptive.continue_words.start: by, to, and, then, point, about, at, of, the, a

endpoint.adaptive.fallback_silence_ms.what: The wait used when no words are available yet (for example with speech-to-text in 'batch' mode, which only produces text at the end). Then it behaves like the plain silence rule.

endpoint.smart_turn.pause_ms.what: How long a pause (milliseconds) before it asks the Smart Turn model 'has the speaker finished?'.
endpoint.smart_turn.pause_ms.higher: Asks less often, so it's a bit slower to finish.
endpoint.smart_turn.pause_ms.lower: Asks sooner, so it's faster, but asks during tiny gaps between words.

endpoint.smart_turn.threshold.what: How sure the model must be (0 to 1) that you've finished before it ends the command.
endpoint.smart_turn.threshold.higher: Waits longer unless the model is very sure: fewer cut-offs, sometimes slower.
endpoint.smart_turn.threshold.start: 0.5 (the value the model was designed for).

endpoint.smart_turn.max_wait_ms.what: A safety limit: if you stay silent this long, it finishes even if the model still thinks you haven't. Stops it waiting for ever after an unusual sentence.

endpoint.ptt_release.fallback_silence_ms.what: Only used if the command was started by the wake word rather than the button (trigger 'both'): there's no button to release, so it falls back to finishing after this much silence.

stt.mode.what: 'batch' transcribes once, after you've finished. 'streaming' transcribes as you speak, so grey text appears live on the page, and the 'adaptive' end-of-turn method can read your words.
stt.mode.start: batch for the most reliable text; streaming to see words live or with 'adaptive'.

stt.partial_every_ms.what: For engines that can't truly stream (Whisper engines, Parakeet on the processor): in streaming mode they re-read everything said so far this often (milliseconds) to update the live text.
stt.partial_every_ms.higher: Less work for the computer, but the live text updates less often.

stt.language.what: The language spoken. The models used here are English ('en').

stt.prompt.what: A list of words you expect to say (robot words, units, the robot's name). Engines that support it (whisper.cpp, faster-whisper) are nudged towards spelling these correctly. Parakeet and Moonshine ignore it.
stt.prompt.start: Truffles, tool, home, joint, gripper, x, y, z, centimetres, millimetres, degrees, up, down, left, right, forward, back, stop.

stt.parakeet.model.what: Which Parakeet model to download and use. Leave as it is.

stt.parakeet.backend.what: Which software runs Parakeet. 'mlx' uses the Mac's GPU (fastest here). 'sherpa_onnx' runs on the ordinary processor, or an NVIDIA card on the lab PC. 'auto' picks for you. 'nemo' needs software not installed.

stt.parakeet.sherpa_model.what: The folder name of the processor version of Parakeet (sherpa_onnx backend only). Leave as it is.

stt.parakeet.threads.what: How many processor cores the sherpa_onnx backend may use. More can be faster, but leaves less for everything else.

stt.parakeet.stream_chunk_ms.what: Streaming mode on the Mac GPU: how much audio (milliseconds) is collected before the live text is updated.
stt.parakeet.stream_chunk_ms.higher: Steadier, more accurate live text, but updates less often.
stt.parakeet.stream_chunk_ms.lower: Livelier, but tests showed garbled words with small chunks.

stt.parakeet.context_left.what: Streaming mode: how much earlier audio the model remembers while updating the live text. Advanced; leave as it is.

stt.parakeet.context_right.what: Streaming mode: how far ahead the model may 'look' before committing to words. Small values made it drop words in testing. Advanced; leave as it is.

stt.parakeet.final_pass.what: Streaming mode: when on, the live text comes from the stream but the FINAL text comes from one extra full read of your whole command (adds about 30–40 ms). Off gives pure streaming, which was less accurate in tests.

stt.whisper_cpp.model.what: Size of the Whisper model. Bigger is more accurate but slower and needs a bigger download. 'tiny.en' misheard simple commands in testing.

stt.whisper_cpp.driver.what: How the prototype talks to whisper.cpp: 'bindings' runs it inside the app (simplest, slightly faster); 'server' runs it as a separate program the app sends audio to.

stt.whisper_cpp.server_url.what: Server mode only: the address the whisper server listens on. Leave as it is.

stt.whisper_cpp.server_bin.what: Server mode only: the name of the whisper server program. Leave as it is.

stt.whisper_cpp.threads.what: How many processor cores whisper.cpp may use.

stt.faster_whisper.model.what: Size of the Whisper model. Bigger is more accurate but slower; on this Mac anything above 'small.en' will be very slow.

stt.faster_whisper.compute_type.what: How precisely the numbers inside the model are stored. 'int8' is fastest on a processor, 'float16' on an NVIDIA card. 'auto' picks for you.

stt.faster_whisper.beam_size.what: How many alternative transcriptions it considers before choosing. More can be slightly more accurate, but is slower.
stt.faster_whisper.beam_size.start: 1 (5 was 14 % slower with the same result in testing).

stt.faster_whisper.threads.what: How many processor cores it may use.

stt.faster_whisper.use_hotwords.what: How the prompt words are given to the model: on = as 'hotwords' (a gentle bias towards those words), off = as an 'initial prompt' (as if they'd been said just before).

stt.moonshine.model.what: Which Moonshine model. The 'streaming' ones are built for live text; bigger is more accurate but slower.

stt.moonshine.update_interval_s.what: Streaming mode: the least time (seconds) between live text updates.
